title: Tax, Invoices and the Books: From Order to Ledger
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/14-tax-invoicing-and-ledger/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (the thesis paragraph, a roadmap, a conclusion paragraph that answers the opening, and Part III's closing); these are listed under open_questions.

know: The three outcomes the commerce system owes finance (the right tax, a valid invoice, books that match the bank) and the documents that carry them, each with its owning system.

The VAT rules that decide a rate: destination rates above the €10,000 One Stop Shop threshold, the reverse charge for EU business buyers with a valid VAT number, and tax-inclusive against tax-exclusive prices.
The ledger entries for a consumer order paid through a payment provider, and why Kestrel & Pine recognizes revenue for goods at delivery.
believe: The shop issues order confirmations; one system per legal entity issues invoices.
Nothing posts to the ledger from a webhook; the ledger is fed from documents.
can_do: Split a tax-inclusive consumer total into net and VAT.
Name the daily and monthly checks that prove the orders, the payouts and the bank agree.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or integration lead who owns the connector between the shop and the ERP (Noor Visser and Ruben Alves at Kestrel & Pine). The finance director who closes the month (Sanne de Wit) is the second reader and should recognize her own problems.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Part II: one owner per product attribute, prices selected once at order placement and frozen, discounts allocated to lines, gift cards and points as liabilities, available-to-promise and the exact commit at checkout.

From the earlier chapters of Part III: checkout creates the order once with its payment pending; the payment provider's four stages and its webhook; one writer and a key for every refund (the Double Refund); the order's one home with three status lines and goods status per shipment, split shipments (the Three-Status Order).
does_not_know: VAT and its rates; tax-inclusive and tax-exclusive prices; the One Stop Shop and its €10,000 threshold; reverse charge and VIES; US sales tax and economic nexus; tax engine.
Invoice content, consecutive numbering, immutability, credit note, retention.
E-invoice, EN 16931, Peppol and its access points, the buyer reference (BT-10), state clearance.
Ledger, debit and credit, revenue recognition under IFRS 15, cut-off, refund liability, breakage, sub-ledger.
Payout report, settlement delay, three-way match, trace or batch reference.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an order shipped in two parcels and invoiced only on 'order complete', the reader names what goes wrong and the invoicing rule that prevents it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order of two items ships in two parcels a week apart; the ERP issues the invoice only when the warehouse reports the whole order complete. Using only this chapter: what goes wrong, and what is the rule?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The invoice waits for the slowest line, so a shipped (and delivered) parcel stays uninvoiced for days. Invoice per shipment at dispatch, keyed on the shipment id, with a daily list of shipped orders that have no invoice.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a return of an invoiced and paid item, the reader names the documents that follow and says the invoice is not changed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer's €199 jacket was invoiced and paid; she returns it for a refund. Using only this chapter: which documents follow, and may the invoice be changed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No: an issued invoice is immutable. A credit note with its own sequential number, referencing the invoice, reverses the jacket line (net and VAT); the refund, sent by the one refund writer, references both, and the three reconcile to zero; the refund appears as a deduction in a later payout.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why a payout differs from a day's sales and how finance shows that nothing is missing.

Finance matches it line by line, using the order number passed to the provider and the batch or trace reference on the bank line, and posts fees from the report; matching totals only cannot find a missing line.

Given a tax-inclusive Dutch consumer total, the reader splits it into net and VAT.

thesis.question: How does an order become tax, an invoice and entries in the books, and what does the commerce system owe finance?
thesis.claim: An order becomes tax, an invoice and ledger entries through documents, not events: the tax is computed from three facts the shop owns (the ship-to address, the product's tax category, and whether the buyer is a consumer or a VAT-registered business) under rates kept in one place for every channel; the invoice is issued at dispatch for each shipment by one system per legal entity, numbered in one consecutive series, never edited and corrected only by a credit note that references it; and the ledger is posted from invoices, credit notes and the payment provider's payout reports. The commerce system owes finance the facts and identifiers those documents need (the tax basis frozen on the order, a shipment confirmation carrying the shipment id, the buyer references an e-invoice must carry, the order number passed to the payment provider, refunds from one writer), so that a monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines explains each difference.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the shop platform's order confirmation is the invoice, that tax is a rate the platform adds at checkout, and that the books can be posted from the platform's payment events as they arrive, with differences found by comparing monthly totals.
thesis.so_what: Order #1052877 sat 'Not invoiced' for six days because the invoice waited for an 'order complete' message that a short pick prevented and no report listed shipped orders without an invoice; the Double Refund's second refund referenced no credit note; Ardennes Trail Co. rejected a Peppol invoice for a buyer reference the B2B portal never asked for. A merchant that accepts the claim makes the ERP the only invoice issuer, invoices per shipment and builds the shipped-not-invoiced list and the refunds-against-credit-notes job first, before an OMS or a PIM.
thesis.how_why: Rates depend on the destination country, the product category and the buyer's status, and change, so rates kept in several channels drift apart. A tax basis recomputed after the address or a rate changes no longer matches what the customer was shown, so the basis is frozen on the order and any difference listed. For goods the supply happens at dispatch, per shipment, so an invoice that waits for the whole order waits for the slowest line. The law requires a consecutive number unique to each invoice and an issued invoice kept unchanged for years, which only one issuing system per legal entity can guarantee. Where two systems can refund, both can refund the same return, so refunds come from one writer. A payout nets payments, refunds, fees and chargebacks from different days, so it never equals a day's sales and can be matched only line by line on identifiers carried from the order.

supporting_claims.claim: The commerce system owes finance three outcomes (the right tax, a valid invoice, books that match the bank), carried by a handful of documents that each have one owning system: the shop issues order confirmations, not invoices, and nothing posts to the ledger from a webhook.

Tax is decided by three facts the shop owns (ship-to address, product tax category, buyer status) under rates kept once for every channel; the figure shown at checkout is a promise and the figure on the invoice is the legal amount, so the basis is frozen on the order or recomputed, and any difference is listed, never left to drift.

The invoice is a legal document: it has prescribed content and a consecutive number, is issued per shipment at dispatch by one system per legal entity, is never edited and is corrected only by a credit note that references it; for an e-invoice the same system holds the transmission status.

The ledger is posted from documents and payout reports, not from payment events, and revenue for goods counts when control passes to the customer (at Kestrel & Pine, at delivery), with expected refunds and unredeemed gift cards held as liabilities.

The books agree with the shop only when invoices and credit notes, payout reports and bank lines are matched line by line on identifiers the order passes along (the order number given to the payment provider, the batch or trace reference on the bank line), with two daily checks: shipped orders without an invoice, and provider refunds against credit notes.

role.contribution: Follows the order into the documents that finance and the tax authorities rely on, extends the one-writer and key rules to invoices and credit notes, and performs the part's closing (the published chapter does not yet do so: it ends with the hand-off to Part IV only).

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene, then owes: Sanne's close and her two questions, then the outcomes and owners that answer them
vat to reconciliation: the documents in the order an order produces them (tax at checkout, invoice at dispatch, ledger entries, the monthly match)

flow.rationale: Sanne's close comes first so every term arrives as part of the answer to her two questions. What the shop owes finance comes next because it names the documents and their owners, which every later section uses. VAT precedes tax at checkout and at invoice because the two moments apply the rules VAT supplies; tax at invoicing leads into the invoice, which must be understood as a legal document before the e-invoice, its structured form, and before the ledger, which is posted from it. Reconciliation follows the ledger because it proves the entries agree with the money. The choices come after all the rules because each choice is a way of applying them, and the stages after the choices because they say which answer fits when. The worked example comes after the choices so that it can show the recommended answers at work (before them, its daily batch, per-shipment invoice and refund-versus-credit-note job would be remedies with no names), and the failures come last because each is read against the rule that prevents it. Moving the owner table after VAT would leave the tax, invoice and ledger sections referring to owners not yet named; moving the invoice after the ledger would post entries from a document the reader has not met; moving reconciliation before the ledger would match entries that have not been explained.

hook.content: A customer pays for an order, but the amount that reaches the merchant's bank is smaller, because the payment provider deducted a fee; a later refund changes it again, and finance has to explain the difference from the tax, the invoice, the fee, the refund and the bank receipt.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has compared a payment with a bank statement knows that the two rarely show the same number on the same day.
bridge.to_topic: For a merchant with hundreds of thousands of orders a year the difference can only be explained if each order leaves documents with identifiers, so the question becomes which documents, issued by which system, and how they are matched.

thesis_statement.text: An order reaches the books through documents, not events: tax decided by facts the shop owns under rates kept once, an invoice per shipment from one issuer that is never edited and corrected only by a credit note, and ledger entries posted from those documents and the payout reports; the shop owes finance the facts and identifiers those documents need, so that a monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines explains each difference.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Sanne's April Close

advances_thesis.how: Gives the case the chapter answers: incidents caused by an invoice that waited, a refund that referenced nothing and an e-invoice missing a field, and the two questions the thesis answers.

flow.rationale: The routine of the close (four routes, each with its own matching rules) first, then the incidents in the order they matter to it, then what is new, then the rejection that turns all of it into two questions: the questions only make sense once the reader has seen what went wrong.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's claim and roadmap, which start from Sanne's April close.
transition_in.introduces: The close itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Sanne de Wit closes April 2027 in the second week of May, and four payment routes must reconcile with the ERP, each with its own matching rules: the online payment service provider's daily batches, the store terminal provider, three marketplaces and 1,100 wholesale accounts on 30-day terms.

evidence.shows: Each route arrives differently and must be matched separately.

sections.heading: What the Commerce System Owes Finance
sections.controlling_idea: The shop owes finance three outcomes (the right tax, a valid invoice, books that match the bank), each carried by documents with one owning system, from which two rules follow: the shop does not issue invoices, and nothing posts to the ledger from a webhook.

advances_thesis.how: States the first supporting claim and the two rules the rest of the chapter applies.

flow.rationale: Outcomes, then the documents that carry them, then the two rules the documents imply, then what the shop must supply to those documents; the rules cannot be stated before the table names the owners, and the inputs only make sense once the rules say the shop does not issue the documents itself.

transition_in.introduces: The outcomes and owners that answer them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In business terms the shop owes finance three outcomes, each enforced by someone outside it: the right tax (tax authorities), a valid invoice (auditors and business customers) and books that match the bank (auditors and the board).
A handful of documents carry those outcomes, and each has one owning system: the order, the tax calculation, the invoice, the credit note, the payment event, the payout report and the ledger entries.

evidence.what: Document entity–owner table: created when, owner (system of record), references.
evidence.shows: Gives each document one owner and names the identifiers that link them.

transition_in.introduces: The documents that carry them and their owners.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two rules follow from the table and carry the rest of the chapter: the shop issues order confirmations, not invoices, and nothing posts to the ledger from a webhook, because the ledger is fed from documents in batches with traceable identifiers.

transition_in.introduces: The two rules it implies.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What the shop owes finance is therefore the facts and identifiers those documents need: the tax basis frozen on the order, a shipment confirmation carrying the shipment id, the buyer references an e-invoice must carry, the order number passed to the payment provider, and refunds from one writer.

transition_in.carries_over: The two rules: the ERP issues invoices and the ledger is fed from documents.
transition_in.introduces: The inputs the shop must supply to those documents.

sections.heading: VAT in Plain Words
sections.controlling_idea: Five facts about VAT decide the rate on a sale: rates differ by country and category, prices are stored tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive, cross-border consumer sales are taxed at the destination, business sales to another EU country are reverse-charged, and the United States has state sales tax instead.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the rules that make the three facts the shop owns decisive and that make rates something to keep in one place.

flow.rationale: The five facts are parallel; rate and basis come first because the cross-border and business rules change which rate and basis apply, and the US comes last as the contrast that explains tax engines.

transition_in.carries_over: The right tax as the first outcome, and the tax calculation document.
transition_in.introduces: What decides that tax.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five facts about VAT carry the chapter.
Rates differ by country and by product category: EU law sets a 15% minimum standard rate and allows reduced rates, and Kestrel & Pine's three markets charge 21%, 19% and 21% as standard.

evidence.what: VAT rates for the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium with sources.
evidence.shows: The destination and the category decide the rate.

transition_in.introduces: The first fact.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's clothing and equipment carry the standard rate everywhere.

transition_in.introduces: Which rate applies to Kestrel & Pine's products.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every stored price must declare whether it includes VAT (Eva's €199) or excludes it (the €95 wholesale price), so that checkout and invoicing compute the same total.

evidence.what: Stripe Tax documentation: inclusive common for B2C outside the US, exclusive for the US, Canada and B2B; tax behavior cannot be changed after creation.
evidence.shows: The basis is a property of the stored price, fixed once.

transition_in.introduces: The second fact: the price's tax basis.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Above €10,000 a year of cross-border EU consumer sales a merchant charges the destination country's VAT and reports it through the One Stop Shop, so Kestrel & Pine must know the destination rate per product category at checkout.

evidence.what: OSS since 1 July 2021, €10,000 threshold; Kestrel & Pine's €8.5 million of Belgian and German online sales.
evidence.shows: The destination, a fact the shop owns, decides the rate.

transition_in.introduces: The third fact: where a consumer sale is taxed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A business sale to another EU country to a buyer with a VIES-checked VAT number carries 0% VAT and the buyer accounts for it (the reverse charge), which is Ardennes Trail Co.'s case.

evidence.what: Your Europe cross-border VAT page: reverse charge and VIES.
evidence.shows: The buyer's status, a fact the shop owns, decides the rate.

transition_in.carries_over: Consumer sales taxed at the destination.
transition_in.introduces: Business sales, where the buyer accounts for the VAT.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The United States has no VAT but state sales taxes that a remote seller must collect above a state's threshold since Wayfair, across thousands of jurisdictions, which is why tax engines exist.

evidence.what: South Dakota v. Wayfair (21 June 2018), $100,000 or 200 transactions; Avalara's '12,000+' jurisdictions claim.
evidence.shows: Rates kept by hand do not scale to that many jurisdictions.

transition_in.introduces: The US contrast.

sections.heading: Tax at Checkout and Tax at Invoice
sections.controlling_idea: The tax shown at checkout is a promise and the tax on the invoice is the legal amount, so the order system either recomputes at invoicing or freezes the checkout basis, and in both cases lists any difference instead of letting the two drift.

advances_thesis.how: Shows why the tax basis is frozen on the order and differences are listed.

transition_in.carries_over: The facts that decide the rate.
transition_in.introduces: The two moments at which they are applied.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The checkout tax is a promise computed from the facts at that moment and the invoice tax is computed when the supply happens (for goods, at dispatch), so the order system must either recompute at invoicing (suited to addresses and baskets that change before dispatch) or freeze the checkout basis and reconcile (suited to a consumer shop that ships whole orders within a day; Kestrel & Pine freezes and lists any difference at invoicing), and never let the two drift silently.

evidence.what: Requirements of the two tax flows: freshness, consistency, speed and fallback.
evidence.shows: Checkout needs speed and a fallback; invoicing needs finality and holds the invoice, not the shipment; the prose names the four columns.

evidence.what: Figure 1: three facts the shop owns and one set of rules decide the tax, once as a promise at checkout and once as the legal amount on the invoice.
evidence.shows: Shows the two moments this section separates.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When a cart mixes rates, shipping and basket-wide discounts must be split across lines, which decides what the credit note for one returned line is worth.

evidence.what: Stripe Tax: proportional allocation and the highest rate.
evidence.shows: There are documented methods, and the choice affects later credit notes.

transition_in.introduces: Tax split across lines with different rates.

sections.heading: The Invoice as a Legal Document
sections.controlling_idea: An invoice has prescribed content and a consecutive number, is never edited, is corrected only by a credit note that references it, is issued per shipment and is kept for years, so one system per legal entity, outliving the shop platform, must issue it.

advances_thesis.how: Derives each architectural rule for invoicing from the law's requirements.

flow.rationale: The law's content first, then each rule derived from it, ending with retention, which settles which system owns the invoice.

transition_in.introduces: The invoice it is computed for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An invoice's content is prescribed by law, and German law requires a consecutive number unique to the invoice.

evidence.what: Belastingdienst invoice requirements; § 14 UStG 'eine fortlaufende Nummer'.
evidence.shows: The content and numbering are legal requirements, not design choices.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three properties follow from that content, and a fourth rule follows from the date of supply; each is an architectural rule.

transition_in.carries_over: The legal content of an invoice.
transition_in.introduces: The rules it imposes on the system that issues it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the number is sequential and gap-free within its series, the system of record assigns it when the invoice is posted, never pre-allocated by checkout or reused from an order sequence with cancellations.

transition_in.introduces: The first: numbering.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An issued invoice is never edited, because finance needs a lasting record of what was billed; an ERP assigns the number on confirmation and then prevents edits.

evidence.what: Odoo 18.0 documentation: draft, number on confirmation, no edits.
evidence.shows: Standard ERP behavior enforces immutability.

transition_in.introduces: The second rule: immutability.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A correction is a credit note that references the invoice, reverses some or all of its lines and has its own number, and a return produces a credit note and a refund that references both, which reconcile to zero.

evidence.what: Odoo: 'issuing a credit/debit note is the only legal method for canceling, refunding, or modifying a validated invoice'.
evidence.shows: The correction is a document, not an edit.

evidence.what: The Double Refund's second refund referenced nothing.
evidence.shows: Without the references the three documents cannot be matched.

evidence.what: Figure 2: locked invoice and its credit note.
evidence.shows: Shows the correction as a separate document.

transition_in.carries_over: An invoice that cannot be edited.
transition_in.introduces: How it is corrected instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine issues one invoice per shipment, dated at its dispatch and keyed on the shipment id, because the supply happens per shipment and an invoice that waits for the whole order waits for the slowest line, as #1052877 did.

evidence.what: #1052877 Not invoiced for six days.
evidence.shows: Invoicing per order caused the incident.

transition_in.carries_over: The three properties of the document.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth rule, from the date of supply: when to issue it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Invoices are kept for seven to ten years, so the invoice must outlive the shop platform, one reason the ERP is its system of record.

evidence.what: Seven years NL basic records; eight years invoices (§ 14b UStG); ten years books (§ 147 AO).
evidence.shows: The invoice outlives any one shop platform.

transition_in.introduces: How long the invoice must be kept, and what that says about its owner.

sections.heading: E-Invoicing at a Glance
sections.controlling_idea: An e-invoice is structured data sent over a network such as Peppol under dates that differ per country, and the system that issues it must also hold its transmission status and archive.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the one-issuer rule to the e-invoice's transmission status.

flow.rationale: Definition, then dates, then ownership; ownership of the status makes sense only once the reader knows an e-invoice is sent and can be rejected.

transition_in.carries_over: The invoice as a legal document.
transition_in.introduces: The same document sent as structured data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An e-invoice is an invoice issued, sent and received as structured data defined by EN 16931, exchanged over Peppol through each side's access point; a PDF by e-mail is not one.

evidence.what: OpenPeppol.
evidence.shows: Defines the network and its access points.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The mandate dates differ per country: Belgium from 1 January 2026, German receipt since 2025 and issuing from 2027 or 2028, a Dutch plan for 1 July 2030 and ViDA's cross-border reporting from 1 July 2030.

evidence.what: einvoice.belgium.be 2024; BMF FAQ; Rijksoverheid 11 September 2026; European Commission ViDA.
evidence.shows: The requirement arrives on dated, country-specific schedules, which is how the Long Fuse is lit.

transition_in.introduces: When it becomes required where.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because an e-invoice has a transmission status a PDF never had, the system that issues it, the ERP at Kestrel & Pine, must hold that status and the archive, and Ardennes Trail Co.'s rejection for a missing buyer reference was a checkout gap, not a finance one.

evidence.what: Ardennes Trail Co.'s rejection: BT-10 never asked for by the B2B portal.
evidence.shows: The shop owes the e-invoice its fields; the issuer owns its status.

transition_in.introduces: What matters for this chapter: ownership.

sections.heading: From Order to Ledger: What Gets Posted
sections.controlling_idea: The ERP posts standard entries from documents, and three accounting rules sit under them: revenue counts when control passes (at Kestrel & Pine, at delivery), a right of return is a liability, and gift cards are liabilities until redeemed.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the postings from documents and the rules that decide when revenue counts.

flow.rationale: The entries first, then the rules that govern them; the cut-off follows the revenue rule because it is that rule applied to an invoice issued at dispatch.

transition_in.carries_over: The documents: invoice, credit note, e-invoice.
transition_in.introduces: What the ERP posts from them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The general ledger records every transaction as a debit and a credit, and the ERP posts a consumer order's invoice, payout, credit note, chargeback and gift-card sale as standard entries from documents; the invoice posts revenue at dispatch and a month-end cut-off aligns it with the revenue rule below.

evidence.what: Journal entries for invoice at dispatch, payout, credit note, chargeback, gift card sold.
evidence.shows: Every entry comes from a document or a payout report.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three accounting rules sit under the table.

transition_in.introduces: The rules that decide their timing and nature.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Under IFRS 15, revenue is recognized when control of the goods passes to the customer, not when the order is placed or paid.

evidence.what: IFRS 15, effective 1 January 2018.
evidence.shows: The accounting moment is control, not order or payment.

transition_in.introduces: The first: when revenue counts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine recognizes consumer and wholesale revenue at delivery, so 'shipped' is the operational milestone, not the accounting one.

evidence.what: Revenue at delivery (D2C) and at delivery to the customer's shop or DC (wholesale).
evidence.shows: Applies the rule to the merchant.

transition_in.introduces: Kestrel & Pine's application of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the invoice is issued at dispatch and revenue counts at delivery, finance adjusts at month end for parcels invoiced but not yet delivered, which is why the shop's daily sales and the ledger never agree to the euro.

evidence.what: Shipped 30 April, delivered 3 May: May revenue on an April invoice.
evidence.shows: The cut-off adjustment in one case.

transition_in.carries_over: Revenue at delivery with the invoice at dispatch.
transition_in.introduces: The month-end adjustment that gap requires.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A right of return is a liability: with a 19% order return rate, expected refunds are estimated at period end.

evidence.what: 19% order return rate.
evidence.shows: Returns are frequent enough to estimate.

transition_in.carries_over: The first rule and its consequences.
transition_in.introduces: The second rule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Gift cards are liabilities until redeemed, with breakage rules that depend on the jurisdiction, and only one system may change a gift-card balance.

evidence.what: A €50 gift card is €50 owed.
evidence.shows: Selling stored value is not revenue.

evidence.what: Figure 3: documents, not events, feed the ledger.
evidence.shows: Summarizes the section's postings.

transition_in.introduces: The third rule.

sections.heading: Reconciliation: Orders, Payouts and the Bank
sections.controlling_idea: Reconciliation proves that the ERP's documents, the payment provider's payout reports and the bank statement agree line by line, which works only when the order number is passed to the provider and the batch or trace reference reaches the bank line.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the match and the identifiers it needs, and the daily job that would have caught the Double Refund.

flow.rationale: Definition, the identifiers and mismatches, then the incident: the fix makes sense only once the reader has the row it belongs to.

transition_in.carries_over: Entries posted from documents and payout reports.
transition_in.introduces: The proof that those entries agree with the money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Reconciliation is proving that two records of the same money agree line by line and explaining every difference; commerce matches three: invoices and credit notes, payout reports and the bank statement.

evidence.what: Figure 4: three strips joined on shared keys with one unmatched line.
evidence.shows: Shows the three-way match.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Payment providers' payout reports list every transaction in a payout and carry the merchant's order reference and a batch or trace reference that matches the bank line, so a merchant that does not pass its order number can reconcile only totals.

evidence.what: Stripe payout reconciliation report and trace_id; Adyen batch-level reconciliation; Mollie settlement report.
evidence.shows: The join keys exist and are documented.

evidence.what: What does not match, why, and how to catch it (five rows).
evidence.shows: Each mismatch has a cause and a check.

transition_in.introduces: The identifiers it runs on.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Double Refund is the table's third row, and its fix had two parts: one writer for refunds and a daily comparison of provider refunds with credit notes.

evidence.what: Double Refund fix from February 2027.
evidence.shows: One writer plus one comparison closes the gap.

transition_in.introduces: The incident it explains and its fix.

sections.heading: The Choices
sections.controlling_idea: Three decisions shape the handoff (where tax is computed, where the invoice is issued, how the ledger learns), each with a simplest, usual and scaled answer, and the usual answer fits Kestrel & Pine's stage.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the rules into choices a merchant makes and recommends one per row.

flow.rationale: Three decisions on the same three answers, then the recommendation; the table needs all three decisions named first.

transition_in.carries_over: The rules for tax, invoices, entries and the match.
transition_in.introduces: The decisions a merchant makes to apply them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three decisions shape the handoff, each with three realistic answers.

Tax can be computed in the shop platform's rate tables, in a tax engine called from checkout and invoicing (necessary for the United States), or in the ERP at invoicing only, which is wrong for a consumer shop.

transition_in.introduces: The first: where tax is computed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The invoice can be issued by the shop platform, the ERP, or an invoicing service in front of several ERPs where some countries run state clearance.

transition_in.introduces: The second decision: where the invoice is issued.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ledger can learn from one posting per paid order, from documents in a daily idempotent batch, or from summary journals with detail in a sub-ledger.

evidence.what: Simplest, usual and scaled answer per decision, with risks.
evidence.shows: Sets the options side by side on the same criteria.

transition_in.introduces: The third decision: how the ledger learns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author recommends the usual answer in each row for a merchant at Kestrel & Pine's stage, including a job that lists orders that should have been invoiced and were not, the job whose absence left the Three-Status Order uninvoiced.

transition_in.carries_over: The three decisions and their answers.
transition_in.introduces: The recommended answer for this merchant.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The shape of the handoff (documents, identifiers, one issuer, one match) does not change with scale; the number of feeds and legal entities does, and with it whether anyone can still match by eye.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the documents and the match are constant and only their number grows.

transition_in.introduces: How the answers change from stage to stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The shape of the handoff does not change with scale, only the number of feeds and legal entities, and Kestrel & Pine's answer is Waypoint's integration standard W5: finance by daily batch with a reconciliation job per flow.

evidence.what: Four stages: typical, necessary, warning signs.
evidence.shows: What grows is the count of feeds and entities, not the shape.

sections.heading: Eva's Order in the Books, and Ardennes Trail Co.'s Peppol Invoice
sections.controlling_idea: Eva's order and Ardennes Trail Co.'s wholesale order show every rule at work: the tax basis frozen on the order, an invoice per shipment at dispatch, a payout matched on the batch reference, a credit note for the exchange, and a reverse-charge Peppol invoice with the buyer reference.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the chapter's rules to one consumer and one business order, step by step.

flow.rationale: Each order in the order its documents appear: tax, payment, invoice, payout, return; then the business order, which reuses the steps with a different tax rule and channel.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eva's €235 order #1072455, placed on 13 April 2027, includes 21% VAT, so its tax basis frozen at checkout is €194.21 net and €40.79 VAT.

evidence.shows: Shows how to split a tax-inclusive total into net and VAT.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: iDEAL moves the money when Eva confirms in her bank app and the provider's webhook marks the order paid, at an assumed fee of about €0.30.

evidence.shows: The fee is what makes the payout smaller than the sale.

transition_in.introduces: The payment seconds later.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On 14 April the warehouse confirms the shipment, the ERP connector's daily batch creates invoice 2027-041822 and posts it, and the revenue is April's because the parcel was delivered on 15 April.

evidence.what: Invoice 2027-041822 (illustrative); entries €235.00 / €194.21 / €40.79.
evidence.shows: The invoice is issued at dispatch from a document batch.

transition_in.introduces: The dispatch and invoice the next day.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The provider's payout two business days after the sales day contains Eva's €235 among some 800 orders net of fees, is posted from the provider's report, and the bank line's batch reference ties the three records together at the May close.

evidence.shows: The batch reference is the key on the bank side.

evidence.what: Figure 5: Eva's order to the ledger with the order number and batch reference as keys.
evidence.shows: Shows the identifiers that let the April close prove agreement.

transition_in.introduces: The payout.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eva's exchange is a credit note referencing invoice 2027-041822 for the jacket line plus a new invoice for size L, with no money moving; in the refund variant the returns portal refunds €199 and the daily job sees one refund and one credit note.

evidence.shows: A correction is a referencing document, not an edit.

transition_in.introduces: The return a week later.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ardennes Trail Co. orders 40 Ridgewalker jackets at €95 (€3,800 excluding VAT) on 21 April 2027; with its VAT number validated in VIES the order is an intra-EU business supply at 0% with the reverse-charge mention, on 30-day terms with no payment provider.

evidence.shows: The reverse charge in a real order.

transition_in.carries_over: A consumer order paid through a provider.
transition_in.introduces: A business order on terms, invoiced over Peppol.

evidence.shows: The one issuer holds the e-invoice's fields and transmission status.

transition_in.introduces: Its invoice at dispatch.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The entry is a €3,800 trade receivable against revenue with no VAT, cleared when the bank transfer quoting the invoice number arrives by 23 May, and the supply is reported in the intra-EU sales listing.

evidence.what: €3,800 trade receivable, no VAT, due 23 May; intra-EU sales listing.
evidence.shows: A business sale posts without VAT and is cleared by a bank transfer quoting the invoice number.

transition_in.introduces: Its posting and payment.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Five failures recur (tax that differs, the invoice that never came, the invoice that came twice, the mandate discovered late, and the refund that doubled with the payout that does not match), and each is detected by a list or job and recovered by a document, never an edit.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that every failure is a document issued by the wrong system, twice or without a reference, and is caught by a comparison.

flow.rationale: Tax first, then the invoice, then the e-invoice, then the money: the order of the chapter's own sections, so each failure is read against the rule that prevents it, and the section ends on the reconciliation that catches what the rules miss.

transition_in.carries_over: The two orders that went right.
transition_in.introduces: What goes wrong and how it is detected.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When invoice VAT differs from checkout VAT, the frozen basis is compared with the invoice at posting; the invoice is right, and any promise of a lower gross price is a commercial discount.

An invoice that waits for a trigger that never arrives leaves an order Delivered and Not invoiced for days; a daily list of shipped orders with no invoice detects it, and an idempotent per-shipment trigger recovers it.

transition_in.introduces: The invoice that never came.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A connector retry that creates two invoices for one order is detected as two invoices with one order number, recovered with a credit note rather than a deletion, and prevented with an idempotency key per shipment.

transition_in.introduces: The invoice that came twice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A mandate discovered late, when a customer rejects a PDF, is detected by a regulatory calendar with an owner, and an access point in front of the ERP is usually faster than the partner's quote; the Long Fuse is a governance failure.

transition_in.introduces: The e-invoice: a mandate discovered late.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The doubled refund and the unmatched payout are the reconciliation table's rows: one refund writer, a daily comparison in both directions and every residual investigated in the same month.

transition_in.introduces: The money failures, already in the reconciliation table.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Sanne's two questions have one answer: the ERP alone issues invoices and credit notes, per shipment and with references, and the proof that orders, payouts and bank agree is a match on identifiers the order passes along; every failure in the chapter is a document issued by the wrong system, twice or without a reference. For the part: Eva's order created while its payment was pending, the Double Refund, the Three-Status Order and the invoice that waited six days look like four problems in four systems and are one: after the cart each fact about an order is first known by a system the merchant does not control and reaches the others by message, so the systems agree only where there is one home with three status lines, one writer per money action or document, a business key on every message and a comparison of every copy with its source.
conclusion.so_what: The remedies are rules, not purchases: the ERP as the only invoice issuer, one invoice per shipment, a daily list of shipped orders without an invoice and a daily comparison of refunds with credit notes, built before an OMS or a PIM; for the part, a read-only provider console, the return id as the refund's key and a decision about the order's home before the OMS was bought. A reader can list the writers, keys and comparisons of their own order flow before any product is discussed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: VAT follows the destination above the OSS threshold and is reverse-charged for EU business buyers; an invoice has prescribed content and a gap-free number, is immutable and corrected only by a credit note; revenue counts at transfer of control; and the e-invoicing dates are set.
